name: The Euclidean Algorithm
statement: To find two numbers' greatest common divisor, keep replacing the larger by its remainder on the smaller.
statementAccent: keep replacing the larger by its remainder on the smaller
meaning: The Euclidean algorithm is an efficient method for computing the greatest common divisor of two integers, the largest number dividing both. It works by repeatedly replacing the larger number with its remainder after division by the smaller, based on the fact that the greatest common divisor of two numbers equals the greatest common divisor of the smaller number and that remainder. Repeating this shrinks the pair quickly, and when the remainder finally reaches zero, the last nonzero value is the greatest common divisor. Described in Euclid's Elements around 300 BC, it is one of the oldest algorithms still in everyday use, a model of algorithmic thinking, and a foundational tool of number theory and computer science.
mechanism: The engine of the algorithm is the identity that the greatest common divisor of two numbers is unchanged when the larger is replaced by its remainder modulo the smaller, because any common divisor of the two also divides that remainder, and vice versa. Applying this repeatedly produces a strictly decreasing sequence of remainders that must reach zero, at which point the previous remainder, dividing everything above it, is the greatest common divisor. The division-with-remainder version is far faster than the older repeated-subtraction form. An extended version tracks additional bookkeeping to express the greatest common divisor as a whole-number combination of the original pair, realising Bezout's identity and yielding modular inverses used in cryptography.

examples.text: For two hundred fifty-two and one hundred five: two hundred fifty-two leaves forty-two, one hundred five leaves twenty-one, forty-two leaves zero, so the greatest common divisor is twenty-one.
A bookkeeping version also finds whole numbers combining the pair to their greatest common divisor, Bezout's identity, the standard route to modular inverses in RSA.
The algorithm is slowest on consecutive Fibonacci numbers, a fact Gabriel Lame proved in 1844, an early result of what became computational complexity theory.

variants.name: The extended Euclidean algorithm
variants.text: The version that additionally computes integers expressing the greatest common divisor as a combination of the inputs, giving Bezout coefficients and modular inverses.

variants.name: The subtraction form
variants.text: The original method that repeatedly subtracts the smaller number from the larger instead of taking remainders, correct but slower than the division-based version.

whyItMatters: The Euclidean algorithm is foundational in both number theory and computer science, the standard way to compute greatest common divisors and, in its extended form, modular inverses that secure the RSA cryptosystem and much of digital communication. It anticipates the whole idea of an algorithm, a finite, mechanical, terminating procedure, and its efficiency analysis, tying the worst case to the Fibonacci numbers through Lame's theorem, is an early landmark of computational complexity. It generalises to polynomials and abstract Euclidean domains, underlies continued fractions, and remains a first example students meet of an ancient method that is still optimal and indispensable today.

working.text: replace the larger number by its remainder on division by the smaller, repeating until the remainder is zero; the last nonzero value is the greatest common divisor.
carry extra bookkeeping to express the greatest common divisor as a whole-number combination of the inputs, giving Bezout coefficients and modular inverses.
use the remainder form rather than repeated subtraction, since it converges in far fewer steps, logarithmic in the size of the numbers.

limits: The algorithm computes the greatest common divisor, not directly the least common multiple, though the latter follows by dividing the product of the numbers by their greatest common divisor. The plain version yields only the divisor; obtaining the Bezout combination or a modular inverse requires the extended version's extra bookkeeping. The subtraction-based form, while correct, can be very slow when the numbers differ greatly, so the efficient method uses remainders. Its speed, logarithmic in the input size, is excellent, but it solves a specific problem and gives no help with the far harder task of fully factoring the numbers into primes.
misreadings: The algorithm finds the greatest common divisor, not the least common multiple, although one can be obtained from the other. It does not factor the numbers into primes, which is a much harder problem; it only extracts their largest shared divisor efficiently. And the fast version uses division remainders, not repeated subtraction; the subtraction form is the historical original and is correct but can be far slower, so equating the algorithm with subtraction understates how quickly the remainder version terminates.
origin: Described in Euclid's Elements around 300 BC, in Book VII for whole numbers and Book X for magnitudes, one of the oldest algorithms in continued use, with its worst-case efficiency analysed by Gabriel Lame in 1844.
